'''Martin David Brasier''' {{Post-nominals|country=GBR|FGS|FLS}} (12 April 1947 – 16 December 2014) was an English [[palaeobiologist]] and [[astrobiologist]] known for his conceptual analysis of [[microfossils]] and [[evolution]] in the [[Precambrian]] and [[Cambrian]].

He was Professor of Palaeobiology at the [[University of Oxford]]<ref>{{cite web| title=Oxford University staff| url=http://www.earth.ox.ac.uk/people/profiles/academic/martinb| access-date=2011-03-02| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110603101944/http://www.earth.ox.ac.uk/people/profiles/academic/martinb| archive-date=3 June 2011| df=dmy-all}}</ref> and Emeritus Fellow of [[St Edmund Hall]]. His research critically examined the context and character of the early fossil record, making use of field mapping, logging, optical [[petrography]], [[stable isotope]] [[geochemistry]], [[confocal microscopy]], NanoSims [[microprobe]]s, and [[lasers]] for high resolution [[3D scanning]] and laser [[Raman spectroscopy]].

== Biography ==
Brasier was born in Wimbledon, London, England. He studied at [[University of Oxford]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |date=2015-01-05 |title=Professor Martin Brasier - obituary |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/11306605/Professor-Martin-Brasier-obituary.html |access-date=2026-09-12 |work=The Telegraph}}</ref> He completed a [[master's degree]] in geology from [[Chelsea College of Science and Technology|Chelsea College]], London (at the time a part of the [[University of London]]). In 1969, he enrolled for doctoral course under the supervision of Tom Barnard the [[University College London]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=McMahon |first=Sean |last2=Cockell |first2=Charles |date=2015-07-20 |title=Martin Brasier (1947–2014): astrobiologist |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S1473550415000178/type/journal_article |journal=International Journal of Astrobiology |language=en |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=527–531 |doi=10.1017/S1473550415000178 |issn=1473-5504|url-access=subscription }}</ref> During 1969 and 1970, he worked as a naturalist on board the [[Royal Navy]] hydrographic survey ships HMS ''Fawn'' and HMS ''Fox''. His duty was mapping the distribution of small algae, protists and marine plants in the [[Caribbean]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Wacey |first=David |date=2015-02-03 |title=A journey in palaeobiology |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo2362 |journal=Nature Geoscience |language=en |publisher= |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=89–89 |doi=10.1038/ngeo2362 |issn=1752-0908|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The fossils he observed there became an inspiration in palaeontology and evolution, as he remarked, "I could see that it is the analysis of interconnections between and within systems that may provide a valuable key for decoding the early history of life."<ref name=":1" /> In 1973, he earned his PhD on the study of Caribbean specimens and ecology from the University College London.<ref name=":2" />

Soon after he received a doctorate, Brasier worked at the [[British Geological Survey]]. Before long he was appointed a lecturer at the [[University of Reading]] where he worked for one year. In 1974, he moved to the [[University of Hull]].<ref name=":3" /> In 1988, he transferred to the University of Oxford as a lecturer in geology under the Department of Life Sciences. Simultaneously he was given a tutorial fellowship at [[St Edmund Hall, Oxford|St Edmund Hall]]. In 1996, he became a reader in earth sciences and, in 2002, a full professor of palaeobiology.<ref name=":1" /> Between 2007 and 2013, he was an Adjunct Professor in the Department of Earth Sciences at the [[Memorial University of Newfoundland]], Canada.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McIlroy |first=Duncan |date=2014-12-19 |title=Professor Martin Brasier, RIP |url=https://www.mun.ca/earthsciences/news-articles/professor-martin-brasier-rip.php |access-date=2026-09-12 |website=Memorial University of Newfoundland |language=en-CA}}</ref> He retired from Oxford in September 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-09-04 |title=Evolution and Early Life: A Celebration of the Career of Martin Brasier on his Retirement |url=https://www.palaeocast.com/evolution-and-early-life/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260611222530/https://www.palaeocast.com/evolution-and-early-life/ |archive-date=2026-06-11 |access-date=2026-09-12 |website=www.palaeocast.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gooday |first=Andrew J. |last2=Gregory |first2=John |date=2016-07-01 |title=Memorial to Martin David Brasier (1947–2014) |url=https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/jfr/article/46/3/221-223/309457 |journal=The Journal of Foraminiferal Research |language=en |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=221–223 |doi=10.2113/gsjfr.46.3.221 |issn=0096-1191|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Brasier died in a car accident near [[Burford]], Oxfordshire, UK, on 16 December 2014.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.earth.ox.ac.uk/news_events/news/department_news/professor_martin_brasier,_rip|title=Professor Martin Brasier, RIP|author=Gideon Henderson|date=17 December 2014|publisher=Department of Earth Sciences, University of Oxford|access-date=17 December 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.seh.ox.ac.uk/news/death-martin-brasier|title=Death of Martin Brasier|author=|date=17 December 2014|publisher=St Edmund Hall, University of Oxford|access-date=18 December 2014|archive-date=18 December 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141218061921/http://www.seh.ox.ac.uk/news/death-martin-brasier|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was survived by his wife, Cecilia, and a daughter and two sons.<ref name=":1" />

==Contributions==
Brasier's contributions include the Brasier–[[J. William Schopf|Schopf]] debate on critical testing of questionable 3460 Ma [[Apex chert]] '[[microfossils]]' at [[NASA]]; work on the earliest well-preserved [[fossils]] of [[cells (biology)]] (3430 Ma [[Strelley Pool]]); the [[pumice]] hypothesis for the [[origins of life]]; mapping the earliest life on land (1000 Ma Torridonian); and the [[palaeoecology]], development and [[evolution]] of [[Ediacaran]] to [[early Cambrian]] organisms.  He was secretary and then leader of the [[International Geoscience Programme]], [[UNESCO]] and [[International Commission on Stratigraphy]] Projects on the [[Precambrian]]-[[Cambrian]] Boundary decision. This defined the base of the [[Phanerozoic]] Eon, [[Palaeozoic]] Era and Cambrian Period at a section in [[Newfoundland and Labrador]] based upon the appearance of the first assemblage of vertical burrowing animal [[trace fossils]], ''[[Treptichnus pedum]]''.<ref>{{cite web| title=Episodes article Precambrian-Cambrian IGCP| url=http://www.episodes.co.in/www/backissues/171/Articles--3.pdf| access-date=2011-03-02| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721153642/http://www.episodes.co.in/www/backissues/171/Articles--3.pdf| archive-date=21 July 2011| df=dmy-all}}</ref> 

The same datum defines the top of the Precambrian and of the [[Proterozoic]] Eon. His own book on the subject, ''Darwin's Lost World'' was published in 2009 as part of the [[Charles Darwin]] centenary celebrations.<ref>{{cite web | author=Martin Brasier | title=Darwin's Lost World at Oxford University Press | url=http://ukcatalogue.oup.com/product/9780199548972.do | access-date=2011-03-02 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120329144304/http://ukcatalogue.oup.com/product/9780199548972.do | archive-date=29 March 2012 | df=dmy-all }}</ref> His sequel, called ''Secret Chambers'', goes in search of the [[Symbiogenesis|symbiotic origins]] of the [[eukaryote]] [[chloroplast]], tracing its evolution through the last two billion years, exploring the ideas of [[Robert Hooke]], [[Elso Barghoorn]], [[Tom Cavalier-Smith]] and [[Lynn Margulis]], and delving into the interval that Brasier dubbed [[Boring Billion|'the Boring Billion']].

==Award and recognition==
*[[Lyell Medal]], Geological Society of London, Burlington House, 2014 (for his research of early life)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lyell Medal |url=https://www.geolsoc.org.uk/About/Awards-Grants-and-Bursaries/Society-Awards/Lyell-Medal |access-date=2022-05-16 |website=The Geological Society of London}}</ref>
*[[Society of Biology]] first book awards nomination 2013 (for Secret Chambers)
